topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Keep the required order of a process in one place while letting related implementations supply selected steps. Worked example: One import sequence with ordinary and doubled units. The base class holds the order and the error boundaries. Derived classes only replace conversion and, optionally, final annotation.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Distinguish an algorithm skeleton from a replaceable step.
Keep input checks and output checks around virtual work.
Explain the limits of nonvirtual orchestration and inheritance.

blocks.text: An abstract base class defines the complete algorithm as a template method. That method calls ordinary shared operations, required virtual steps, and optional virtual hooks in a fixed order. A concrete subclass supplies the varying steps. The base algorithm calls into the subclass at those designated points. Here template means a planned sequence; it does not refer to C++ template parameter syntax.

cards.question: What problem does Template Method address?
cards.answer: Keep the required order of a process in one place while letting related implementations supply selected steps. Worked example: One import sequence with ordinary and doubled units. The base class holds the order and the error boundaries. Derived classes only replace conversion and, optionally, final annotation.

cards.question: What is Template Method?
cards.answer: A base-class operation that fixes a sequence while letting derived classes replace selected steps.

cards.question: What is Hook?
cards.answer: An optional extension point with a useful default or an empty default action.

cards.question: What is Postcondition?
cards.answer: A rule that must be true when an operation successfully returns.

cards.question: What is Name hiding?
cards.answer: A derived declaration prevents ordinary lookup from finding a same-named base declaration; it is not necessarily an override.

cards.question: Why does run validate all raw input before calling convert once?
cards.answer: That is the workflow contract. With {3,-1}, no conversion may run before rejection. Combining the loops would change observable behavior for a step with side effects.

cards.question: Does an optional hook mean subclasses may reorder the process?
cards.answer: No. A hook changes behavior at its designated point. The template method retains the call order; suffix runs only after all conversions succeed.

cards.question: Why is run nonvirtual while convert is virtual?
cards.answer: The base class fixes the workflow order. Subclasses supply a conversion step without replacing the shared validation, formatting and postcondition checks.

cards.question: What is the difference between a required step and an optional hook?
cards.answer: convert is pure virtual and must be supplied. suffix has a default empty result, so subclasses may keep it or override it.

cards.question: Why validate converted output if raw input was valid?
cards.answer: A derived hook can still violate its contract. BrokenImport demonstrates that valid raw input alone does not guarantee a valid result.

cards.question: Could passing a conversion callable be simpler than inheritance?
cards.answer: Yes, especially for one small varying step. Template Method is useful when a base workflow coordinates several overridable steps or an existing inheritance framework requires them.

cards.question: Why should expected-output comparison preserve the trailing space?
cards.answer: The supplied formatter intentionally emits it. Trimming output can hide formatting regressions and make the printed contract differ from what the program actually returns.

cards.question: Does const run forbid changes anywhere in the program?
cards.answer: No. It constrains ordinary mutation through this object. A derived hook could still touch mutable or external state; such effects need their own documented contract.

cards.question: What regression test protects a new subclass from bypassing input rules?
cards.answer: Call it with empty input and with 101, and require the same base exceptions as older subclasses. Successful new output alone does not verify the inherited gates.

topics.title: Two imports must follow the same rules
topics.summary: An import tool receives whole-number readings from 0 through 100. One input source already uses the desired units. Another source needs every value doubled. Each result is a space-separated string; the doubled form ends with scaled. Reject an empty input and reject any out-of-range reading. A bad reading late in the batch must be found before any conversion begins. The caller must receive a complete string or an exception, never a partly formatted result.

blocks.text: A simple implementation writes one loop for the ordinary input and copies it for the doubled input. The excerpt shows the ordinary conversion after validation. This is easy to understand at first. But when the team adds a full-batch validation rule, both import functions need the same repair. If only one is repaired, the sources obey different rules even though their only intended difference is a unit conversion.

discussion.question: What maintenance problem follows from copying the entire import workflow for each conversion?
discussion.answer: A validation or ordering repair must be repeated in every copy. One workflow may drift and accept inputs another rejects. The design needs to preserve the common order while varying only selected steps.

topics.title: The limitation calls for one fixed sequence
topics.summary: The repeated sequence is validate all inputs, convert each value, check each converted value, and finish the string. The differing step is how one valid integer becomes another. The Template Method pattern places the sequence in a base class and lets derived classes supply selected steps. Here Import::run is the template method. The word template means a shared plan of steps; it does not refer to C++ template parameters.

blocks.text: convert is a required step: every concrete import must supply it. suffix is an optional hook: the base implementation returns an empty string, so an ordinary import need not override it. DoubleImport changes both conversion and suffix. Optional does not mean uncontrolled. A hook must still obey the documented contract and must not quietly perform a second import or change shared input.

topics.title: Where control moves and where it does not
topics.summary: The caller invokes run. run first walks the full input to check every raw value. Only after that pass succeeds does it create the local stream and call convert for each input. The virtual call selects the actual derived implementation. Control returns to run, which checks that the result lies from 0 through 200 and appends it. The final suffix call happens once after the loop. The base therefore owns the order while the derived class owns a small part of the meaning.

blocks.text: The two passes are deliberate. In a one-pass implementation, convert(3) could run before discovering -1 in the next position. For our pure conversion methods that would not change external state, but the order would violate the stated guarantee. A future conversion with an audit counter would expose that difference. Define order before optimizing away a pass. The cost is one extra linear walk; it does not copy the vector.

input is a const reference, so run borrows existing readings. Each raw loop variable is an integer copy. value is another local integer, held const because the result should not change after the conversion call. The stream owns the characters accumulated so far. Its exception mask enables badbit and failbit exceptions: an output failure must throw rather than silently leave a partial stream result. result.str() returns a string value. If conversion throws or violates the result range, stack cleanup destroys the local stream, and no partial string is returned. This does not undo outside effects a derived step might already have made.

topics.title: A skeleton is a contract, not a security barrier
topics.summary: run is nonvirtual, so calls through Import use this exact sequence. A derived class can declare a same-named nonvirtual member and hide it for calls made through that derived type. That is name hiding, not overriding. Our final concrete classes do not do so, and normal clients use the inherited run. If a framework needs the compiler to forbid overriding an already virtual public entry point, virtual plus final is an available design. It still does not prevent unrelated methods from doing other work.

blocks.text: Protected access lets derived classes implement and use steps without advertising them as normal public operations. A derived override may be private, as it is here: access checking uses the base declaration at the call inside Import, and virtual dispatch can reach the private override. override asks the compiler to verify that the method truly matches a virtual base declaration. It prevents mistakes such as accidentally omitting a trailing const and introducing a different function.

At compilation, types and signatures are checked. During execution, run chooses step implementations from the actual import object. The object must already be fully constructed. Do not call a pure virtual conversion from the base constructor to “test” it: construction-time virtual behavior does not act like a call on a completed derived object. Validate construction data without relying on not-yet-constructed derived behavior.

topics.title: When composition gives a better boundary
topics.summary: Template Method fits a family of closely related processes whose ordering is stable and whose variation belongs in a few well-defined steps. Its cost is inheritance coupling: changing the base sequence changes every derived import. Adding many hooks can make the sequence hard to reason about because every empty-looking call may run unknown derived work.

blocks.text: If callers need to exchange the conversion while keeping the same importer object, inject a Strategy instead. If there are just two lines of differing math, pass a callable to one ordinary function. If whole workflows differ in ordering, forcing them into one inherited skeleton may hide the true differences. Choose a stable sequence first, then decide how much extension it needs.

This example checks both sides of the extension point: raw values are preconditions, converted values are postconditions, which are rules that must hold when a step returns. Runtime range checks catch some bad implementations, such as BrokenImport returning 201. They cannot prove that doubled units have the right business meaning. Keep value-based tests alongside these general contract checks.

cards.answer: Import::convert. Require each concrete implementation to supply essential varying behavior.

cards.answer: Import::suffix. Offer a default behavior that a subclass may replace when needed.

cards.answer: PlainImport and DoubleImport. Supply specialized steps while using the inherited workflow.

topics.title: Exercise 21.6: Justify a decision
topics.summary: A reviewer wants validation and conversion combined to avoid the second pass. Explain whether that preserves this chapter’s contract.

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: Consider a bad final raw value and a conversion that records calls.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: It does not preserve the guarantee that no conversion runs before all raw values are valid. For {3,-1}, a combined pass converts 3 first. Approve the optimization only after deliberately weakening that guarantee, proving pure conversion is sufficient, and updating tests and documentation. Keeping two passes is the correct answer under the current requirements.

blocks.title: Main points
items: Template Method means a shared algorithm sequence, not a C++ generic template.
Required steps and optional hooks have different extension duties.
Preconditions and postconditions belong around variable work.
Nonvirtual orchestration fixes calls through the base but does not prevent name hiding.
Use composition when behavior must vary independently of inheritance.

concepts.definition: A base-class operation that fixes a sequence while letting derived classes replace selected steps.
An optional extension point with a useful default or an empty default action.
A rule that must be true when an operation successfully returns.
A derived declaration prevents ordinary lookup from finding a same-named base declaration; it is not necessarily an override.

steps.why: The derived step runs, then the base checks and appends.

The hook is called once after the loop.

workshop.pitfall: Validate raw values only as they are converted. With {3,-1}, convert(3) runs before -1 is rejected. One pass changes the required order even if the final function still throws.

discussion.question: One import has a fixed sequence with two specialized steps. Another application must switch among many conversions in the same running object. Choose Template Method or Strategy for each.
discussion.answer: Template Method fits the stable inherited sequence. Strategy fits runtime replacement inside one context. A callable is an even smaller option when the replaceable conversion is the only varying operation; neither pattern is mandatory merely because two functions differ.
discussion.hint: Separate changing object behavior from defining a related type.

workshop.alternative: A function accepting a conversion callable would reduce inheritance and suit a single variable step. A Strategy member is preferable if a running import object must exchange its conversion at runtime.
workshop.design: The base class holds the order and the error boundaries. Derived classes only replace conversion and, optionally, final annotation.
invariants: Every raw value is checked before the first convert call.
Only checked converted values enter the local output stream.
suffix runs once after all conversions succeed.
workshop.maintenance: A single validation repair benefits every importer using run. Keep hooks narrow so a future source format does not require reading an entire inheritance tree to understand one import.
workshop.verification: main verifies both complete strings, raw and converted boundaries, unchanged input, empty and negative input rejection, and a deliberately defective step whose violation is caught. BrokenImport is exercised only through a checked path. Stream failure exceptions are enabled, but allocation and stream-failure injection are not tested. No test claims to roll back external effects in future steps.
